newsitem.title: UK: BA faces turbulent shareholders meeting.
newsitem.headline: BA faces turbulent shareholders meeting.

text.p: British Airways, locked in a bitter pay dispute which has cost the company tens of millions of pounds, looks set for a another turbulent shareholders' meeting on Tuesday.
Demonstrations of disgruntled employees are likely to take place, although trade unions said they don't plan any protests as talks with BA continue after cabin crew went on strike last week.

Normal service would not resume until later this week, BA said earlier, after schedules were thrown into disarray and passengers left stranded across the globe during a 72-hour strike which ended on Friday.
Cabin crew leaders will come up with proposals later this week in a bid to solve the dispute over pay and conditions, prompted by a BA plan announced in September to save 42 million pounds.
A walkout by caterers was averted earlier on Monday as BA's ground staff decided to seek further talks over the sale of the airline's catering operation at London Heathrow airport.
The planned divestment and the cost-cutting package affecting cabin crew are all part of BA's ambitious strategy to become a truly global airline.
The cornerstone of this grand plan is a highly controversial alliance with American Airlines.
The planned link-up has caused an uproar among rival airlines and sparked a protracted round of negotiations with competition authorities on both sides of the Atlantic.
Shareholders will be keen to hear what direction the talks are taking after BA already accused authorities of dragging their feet.
The company last month threatened to abandon the American Airlines alliance if regulatory approvals failed to come through before November.
The European Union, meanwhile, has already ruled out a decision before September after talks between Britain and the U.S. were suspended in May following the change of government here.

Both Britain and the U.S. have made approval of the BA-American Airlines alliance conditional on a so-called "open skies" pact between both countries, which requires Britain to open up London's Heathrow airport to greater competition.
A related issue which is also lurking at the background of tomorrow's shareholders' meeting is the lawsuit filed last month by Florida-based Laker Airways Inc.
Owner Freddie Laker is accusing BA of using its dominant position at London's Gatwick airport to prevent his smaller airline from getting desirable take-off and landing slots.
Earlier this month, BA rejected mediation, saying there were no grounds for Laker's lawsuit.

The Laker row is just another controversy likely to feature at Tuesday's meeting. It has all the ingredients for a lively spectacle, but will probably fail to produce deeper insights into BA's strategies or financial health, analysts said.
"I'm not going and that tells you enough on how important the meeting is to me," said one industry watcher.
